proposals.name: Engages the merits versus requesting only procedural relief
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the comment addresses the substance of what the agency proposed, as opposed to asking for administrative accommodation. 10 = the comment takes a position on the proposal itself and gives reasons a decision-maker could act on. 5 = a genuine substantive point wrapped inside a larger administrative request. 0 = the entire comment is a procedural ask (extend the comment period, grant more time, schedule a meeting, fund a program) with no evaluation of the proposal's content; describing how long or complex the proposal is does not count as substance.
proposals.rationale: R17, R25, R28, R44 and R54 are all pure comment-period extension requests and the scorecard ranks them at the very top of the pool (card_pct .949-.990) while the dense model ranks them near the bottom (.272-.346 and lower). Extension letters are polished, correctly addressed, well organized and carry one clean ask, so a bank keyed to form credits them heavily; none of them evaluates the rule. R59 and R50 are almost entirely merits and sit at card .189 and .119.

proposals.name: Substance remaining after letterhead, rosters and scan noise
proposals.instruction: Mentally delete everything that is not argument: letterhead, addresses, board-member lists, phone and fax numbers, OCR garbage, cover notes, repeated headers, signature blocks. Score only what remains. 10 = after stripping the furniture a specific, reasoned position on the proposal remains, even if the surrounding document is visually a mess. 5 = a modest but real claim survives. 0 = after stripping the furniture nothing remains but a greeting, an organizational self-description and a bare 'we support' or 'we oppose'. Do not reward or penalize how clean the transcription is.
proposals.rationale: R41 is roughly two hundred lines of mangled board-of-directors OCR wrapped around a short but real claim that thiamethoxam products displaced older insecticides on effectiveness and safety grounds; the scorecard puts it at .248 while the dense model puts it at .989. R47 and R49 have the same shape - badly degraded scans carrying concrete demands and grower economics - at card .365 and .142. R13 is literally an index of filenames at card .205. Conversely R02 and R56 are clean, orderly documents whose strippable content is mostly self-description.

proposals.name: Supplies information the agency cannot obtain elsewhere
proposals.instruction: Score whether the comment injects facts into the record that are private to the commenter - their own operations, costs, inventory, catch, inspections, or direct field observation - rather than restating material the agency already possesses. 10 = contains at least one concrete first-party factual claim the agency could not look up on its own. 5 = first-party experience asserted only in general terms. 0 = every factual claim is a restatement of the agency's notice, public statistics, published studies, or statutory text.
proposals.rationale: R18 reports that FedEx's fleet contains none of the affected HPT disks or compressor spools, R42 supplies an American Samoa annual average catch of 21,139 lb and a count of three to six full-time fishermen, R26 reports which Ipeco seat part numbers sit on which UPS fleets. All are dense-high against card .095-.147. R04, R37, R46 and R57 are well-written but every fact in them is sourced from NOAA, published reports, statutes or the academic literature, and all four are dense-low with card .739-.938.

proposals.name: Concrete operational exposure to this specific action
proposals.instruction: Score how precisely the commenter locates themselves inside the scope of the proposal. 10 = the text names the specific equipment, part numbers, acreage, tonnage, fleets, permits, plans, products or transactions of the commenter that the proposal would actually reach. 5 = the commenter is plainly a regulated party but describes exposure only in category terms. 0 = the commenter's relationship to the action is a general interest, a mission statement, or a membership count, with no operational detail.
proposals.rationale: R36 names the twenty-one 747-400 airplanes affected and the exact Boeing document revision, R18 names the specific disks and spools, R49 sets the 43 million pound restriction against 200+ million pounds of imported product, R42 sets the 13,000 lb interim limit against actual catch. These run dense .693-.959 against card .046-.220. R46 and R32 substitute membership counts and mission language for operational detail and sit dense-low or card-high.

proposals.name: Short decisive comment from a directly exposed party
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the comment's length is proportionate to what it has to say, given who is saying it. 10 = a short comment that states a definite position on a matter the commenter is unambiguously exposed to, and then stops - no padding, no restatement of the notice. 5 = length roughly matched to content. 0 = a long comment whose length comes from self-description, restatement of the agency's own notice, or hedged generalities, so that very few distinct claims are made per page. Length by itself is neither good nor bad; the ratio is what is scored.
proposals.rationale: R33 is one sentence from Boeing concurring in an airworthiness directive on its own airplane and R36 is a short United Airlines concurrence naming its affected fleet; both are dense-high (.947, .898) at card .333 and .220, suggesting the scorecard reads brevity as thinness. R03 and R15 are two-sentence comments that each carry exactly one definite claim, at card .022 and .046. R02 and R56 are long, orderly and card-high while making few distinct claims.

proposals.name: Contests the proposal's premise, necessity or legal basis
proposals.instruction: Score whether the comment challenges something the agency has assumed, rather than only asking for accommodation inside the agency's frame. 10 = names a premise, justification, legal authority, or design choice in the proposal and gives a reason it is wrong, unsupported, or self-defeating. 5 = accepts the frame but pushes back on one parameter. 0 = accepts the frame entirely and asks only for flexibility, funding, time, or leniency.
proposals.rationale: R07 argues the exemption removal is an entry barrier engineered through the regulatory process by a competing committee, R50 states that the practical utility of FDA's study is unclear and attacks its sampling frame, R52 points out that the 25-54 age restriction is given no stated rationale, R42 disputes that the stock assessment captures the real fishery. These run dense .693-.959 against card .086-.227. R02 and R24 accept the frame and ask for flexibility or funding and are card-high (.776, .895).

proposals.name: Names who bears the cost and who gains
proposals.instruction: Score whether the comment identifies the incidence of the proposal: which specific parties gain, which bear the burden, and by what mechanism the effect is transmitted. 10 = traces effects to named classes of parties with a stated transmission path (price pass-through, market access, exposure, competitive advantage, compliance recordkeeping). 5 = asserts that some group is harmed or helped but supplies no mechanism. 0 = speaks of burden or benefit only in the abstract.
proposals.rationale: R49 traces restriction costs from handlers back into grower prices while foreign concentrate takes the shelf space, R07 identifies California desert grape producers as the beneficiaries of a barrier to importers, R27 reports that 97 percent of fatalities in these two-vehicle crashes fall on passenger-vehicle occupants. All are dense-high at card .142, .115 and .342. R02 asks only that regulatory burden be minimized in general and R44 asserts review burden with no incidence at all, both card-high.

proposals.name: Shows evidence of having read this particular document
proposals.instruction: Score how strongly the text demonstrates first-hand contact with the specific proposal rather than with its subject matter. 10 = quotes, cites or names a particular section, paragraph, option, table, form box, or enumerated agency question and responds to it. 5 = accurately characterizes the proposal's general effect without pinpointing anything. 0 = the comment discusses the topic but could be pasted unchanged into any docket on that subject.
proposals.rationale: R30 singles out the specific addition of U.S. No. 1 grades for non-orange carrots, R59 works through Form 1098-F box numbers and the gap between the preamble and proposed 26 CFR 1.6050X-1(e), R52 identifies the unexplained 25-54 age band; these are dense .741, .803 and .844 at card .069, .189 and .140. R08 and R04 discuss their policy areas competently but contain nothing tied to the particular document, and both are card-high (.876, .936) and dense-low.

proposals.name: Individually composed rather than campaign-template text
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the text was written for this submission by this writer. 10 = phrasing, examples and concerns are idiosyncratic and could not have been supplied by an organizer. 5 = a template body with a substantive personal addition. 0 = recognizable campaign language throughout - stock characterizations of named officials, prefabricated paragraphs of statistics about the policy area, an opening line asserting that the issue matters - with no particular detail originating with the writer.
proposals.rationale: R04 reads as an action-alert text complete with supplied decline percentages and mortality figures, and R08 bolts a one-line personal assertion onto standard advocacy paragraphs; card ranks them .936 and .876 while the dense model ranks them .023 and .031, so the scorecard appears to be crediting the organizer's craft to the commenter. R01 shows the seam directly: a template methane letter followed by a personal addendum that contradicts the letter it is attached to.

proposals.name: Stays on the docket rather than drifting into grievance
proposals.instruction: Score topical discipline. 10 = every paragraph bears on the action under comment. 5 = one clearly bounded digression. 0 = the bulk of the text is a personal grievance, an institutional narrative, or an advocacy topic that belongs in a different proceeding, connected to this docket only by a thin framing sentence.
proposals.rationale: R23 spends most of its length on a testing vendor's cancelled appointments and refund practices inside a comment on a proposed regulation, and R55 is a personal account of grant-funded student support offered as a comment on a grant extension; both are card-high (.676, .903) and dense-low (.037, .210). R01 drifts from methane standards into the Paris Agreement and nuclear power. R21 and R59 never leave the provision at issue.

proposals.name: Attaches magnitude to the burden or harm claimed
proposals.instruction: Score whether quantities are supplied where the argument depends on them. 10 = the comment states numbers - thresholds, volumes, counts, dollars, durations, rates - and uses them in its reasoning rather than as decoration. 5 = one supporting number, otherwise qualitative. 0 = the argument turns on how large a burden or harm is, but no magnitude is ever given.
proposals.rationale: R59 argues the $600 statutory reporting threshold is far too low and proposes at least $50,000, R49 contrasts a 43 million pound domestic restriction with 200+ million pounds of foreign product, R27 cites 5,700 deaths, 155,000 injuries and $66 billion. Card ranks these .189, .142 and .342. R44 and R25 assert that expert review will take substantial time without ever sizing it, and R02 asks for maximum flexibility with no numbers at all, all at card .949-.963.

proposals.name: Builds a record: exhibits, indexes, citations, companion filings
proposals.instruction: Score the evidentiary apparatus the comment brings with it. 10 = footnoted sources, an index of attachments, named studies with authors, prior submissions in this or a related docket, or explicit cross-references to companion comments. 5 = one or two named sources. 0 = no sources, attachments or cross-references of any kind.
proposals.rationale: R13 is nothing but a master index of dozens of attached studies and agency documents assembled for a CAFE docket, and R27 footnotes NHTSA, FMCSA, BLS and IIHS across a fifty-year history of agency inaction; R45 forwards companion NCGA and Missouri Corn comments. Card ranks these .205, .342 and .357 while the dense model ranks them .942, .964 and .945 - consistent with a scorecard scoring the visible page rather than the package that page introduces.

proposals.name: Argument carried by specifics, not by asserted credentials
proposals.instruction: Score where the persuasive weight actually sits. 10 = the commenter's expertise is demonstrated through the technical content itself, with credentials mentioned briefly or not at all. 5 = credentials are stated and then substantially used. 0 = a prominent recitation of degrees, ratings, titles, years of service or standing, followed by claims that rest on that standing rather than on evidence, or by rhetorical assertion and invective in place of data.
proposals.rationale: R16 opens with thirty years of charter fishing and a marine biology degree, then argues from bag limits it concedes are only 'certainly low' and from 'it makes NO SENSE', with no figure anywhere; R38 lists ratings, two degrees and 6000 flight hours, asks several fair questions, then attributes the proposal to a '406 ELT mafia' and an ongoing 'vendetta'. Both are card-high (.870, .805) and dense-low (.164, .095). R59 and R26 never establish who they are beyond the letterhead and argue entirely from regulatory text and part numbers.

proposals.name: Self-contained: who is commenting, on what, asking what
proposals.instruction: Score whether a reader holding only this text can recover three things: who is commenting, which action is being commented on, and what change is requested. 10 = all three are recoverable from the text itself. 5 = two of the three. 0 = the text is a fragment, an annotation set, or a bare question list with no identification of the commenter, no docket or subject anchor, or no discernible request.
proposals.rationale: R53 is a page-by-page set of well-informed technical annotations with no commenter, no docket reference and no stated request, and the dense model ranks it lowest in the entire slice (.008) against card .811; R60 is three unattributed questions and R31 is a single unanchored ask, at card .845 and .701 with dense .031 and .041. R42 and R18 make all three explicit and are dense .959 and .693.

proposals.name: Content exceeds its packaging rather than the reverse
proposals.instruction: Score the balance between presentational apparatus and delivered content. 10 = plain presentation carrying dense, non-redundant content. 5 = form and content matched. 0 = elaborate apparatus - numbered comment-response tables, formal headings, duplicated cover-and-attachment text, checkbox forms - wrapped around thin, purely editorial, or repeated content. Judge the apparatus against what it actually delivers, not against a general standard of tidiness.
proposals.rationale: R51 presents ten comments in a formal comment-response table whose displayed entry is a checked 'Editorial' wording change, and R21 reproduces its entire three-sentence request verbatim twice, once as portal text and once as the attached letter; card ranks them .986 and .993, the two highest in the slice, while the dense model ranks them .173 and .129. R35 shows the same shape at card .934 with dense .075. R59 has no apparatus whatsoever and is dense .803 at card .189.

proposals.name: Sheer volume of text
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much text the comment contains, measured as extent only. Anchors: 0 = one or two sentences (a few dozen words); 3 = a single short paragraph; 5 = roughly one page of prose; 8 = several pages; 10 = a very long submission that continues well past a page or two, or whose pasted-in attachment body runs on at length. Count everything present in the item: cover note, address blocks, quoted regulatory text, footnotes, rosters, and appended attachment text. Do NOT judge whether the length is warranted, whether the writing is efficient, or whether anything useful is said. You are measuring bulk, not merit, and a very short comment is not thereby worse.
proposals.rationale: Length is the canonical text-only nuisance: it is cheap to produce, is largely set by whether an attachment was pasted into the record, and is mechanically available to any model. The slice spans two-sentence items (R35 'User fee rates need to be adjusted appropriately...', R58 on carrot grades, R54 on neonicotinoids) and multi-page institutional filings (R34 Murray Energy, R42 Truck Safety Coalition, R44 NRDC batch index). Because both halves of the disagreement contain both very short and very long items (short R32 and R43 alongside short R21 and R30), any model weight on bulk is weight on a channel that is orthogonal to what is actually argued.

proposals.name: Scanned-attachment ingestion signature: stub, OCR garble, page furniture
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much of the item bears the marks of having been filed as a scanned or PDF attachment and then machine-transcribed, rather than typed directly into the comment box. Count, as extent: (a) a short transmittal stub at the top such as 'See attached', 'See attached file(s)', 'Please find attached', optionally preceded by a bare digit; (b) character-level transcription corruption -- dropped or doubled letters, letters substituted for each other, mangled signatures, ligature errors; (c) page furniture carried through from the source document -- 'Page 2 of 8', repeated date/addressee headers, fax and phone footers, stray line breaks mid-sentence; (d) duplication, where the same paragraph appears once in the cover note and again in the attachment body. Anchors: 0 = clean typed prose with none of these; 5 = clear stub plus page headers but readable text; 10 = pervasive corruption and page furniture that makes stretches hard to read. Do NOT judge whether the corruption makes the comment worse, and do NOT penalise or reward the author for it -- you are scoring how much of this signature is visible, nothing else.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. The unseen factor is how the document physically reached the docket -- faxed or mailed paper and scanned PDFs get OCR'd, inline web-form text does not -- and it leaves a loud textual fingerprint. R02 shows it as a mangled signature ('/)~ __ fivJ-', 'Gro~') and 'It_appears'; R09 (UPS Airlines) is corrupted throughout ('lowe e023 ups', 'flet', 'samme', 'ofthe'); R10 shows systematic character substitution ('ltr/ater Quality Standards', 'Ambient' rendered 'Ambientt'-style, 'W'atershed'); R33 renders every W as VV ('VVildEarth', 'FVVS'); R29's board roster is nearly unreadable. This is an artifact of the pipeline and of filing habits, not of the author's reasoning, yet it is a strong, stable, learnable text signal, and it co-varies with era and with paper-filing organisations. Tagged not-mixed because the corruption itself is injected downstream of the author and cannot make the underlying argument better.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission medium (paper/fax/scanned PDF attachment versus native electronic text entry), plus the corpus's own OCR pipeline

proposals.name: Comment's operative ask is a procedural scheduling request
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the comment's operative request is procedural or scheduling in nature rather than an engagement with the substance of the proposal. Procedural asks include: requesting an extension of the comment period by a stated number of days; asking for a public meeting, hearing, or reopening; asking that a previously filed comment be withdrawn or replaced; asking for more time to consult members or experts. Anchors: 0 = the comment makes no procedural request at all and speaks only to the merits; 5 = a procedural request appears alongside substantive comment; 10 = the entire document is a procedural request, with the surrounding text serving only to justify why more time or process is needed. Do NOT judge whether the request is reasonable, well-argued, or appropriate, and do NOT treat a procedural comment as inferior -- score only how much of the document is that speech act.
proposals.rationale: This is a speech-act/topic marker, not a quality property: an extension request is a highly stereotyped genre with a fixed skeleton (identify the notice, describe the association, note complexity, request N days, thank the agency). Five items in the slice are exactly this genre -- R16 (American Chemistry Council, 30 days), R26 (Philip Morris International, 90 days), R37 (Consumer Brands Association, 60 days), R41 (Al Fakher, 90 days), R47 (American Frozen Food Institute, 30 days) -- and all five sit in the same half of the disagreement, which is what a strong spurious channel looks like. The genre is uniform in form regardless of who files it or how well they later argue the merits, so the marker travels independently of substantive quality.

proposals.name: Density of technical identifiers and legal citation strings
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the density of formal identifier strings in the text. Count: part numbers and model designations (e.g. alphanumeric strings like 'P/N MA30A1017', 'V2527E-A5', 'GE90-115B'); service bulletin, standard, and directive numbers ('SB 747-25-3653 Revision 1', 'ISO/IEC 17025', 'ASTM E1527-21'); statutory, regulatory and Federal Register citations ('21 CFR part 225', '16 U.S.C. 1539(j)(2)(A)', '85 Fed. Reg. 70146'); and docket, RIN and project identifiers. Anchors: 0 = no such strings anywhere; 3 = only the docket number in a subject line; 6 = several per page, woven into the argument; 10 = identifier strings are a large fraction of every paragraph. Do NOT judge whether the citations are correct, apt, or well-integrated, and do NOT treat their presence as expertise -- you are counting how much identifier text is on the page.
proposals.rationale: Identifier density is essentially a subject-matter marker: aviation airworthiness dockets and tax dockets force these strings into the text regardless of how thoughtful the comment is. R30 (Japan Airlines) is five lines long and still carries 'P/N MA30A1017', 'Boeing SB 777-28A0034 Rev. 3' and two AD numbers; R52 (International Aero Engines) is little more than a list of engine model designations; R28 (FedEx) and R09 (UPS Airlines) are dense with SB and part numbers; R15 (Prudential) does the same with 'Treas. Reg. 1.6049-5(c)(5)' and section references. A model can learn 'looks like an FAA/IRS docket' from these strings alone, which is a topic prior, not a perception of quality.

proposals.name: Quantified constituency and market-scale self-description
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the comment quantifies the size, reach, or market position of the entity on whose behalf it is written. Count explicit numbers attached to the filer's own scale: membership counts, employee counts, revenue or premium volume, market share percentages, numbers of customers, policies, accredited bodies, or affiliated organisations, and lists of the constituencies represented. Anchors: 0 = no self-description of scale at all; 3 = a bare unquantified identification ('we are a trade association representing the industry'); 6 = one or two quantified scale claims; 10 = a full paragraph or more of quantified scale and market-share claims. Do NOT judge whether the claimed scale is impressive, relevant, or true, and do NOT treat a small or unstated constituency as a defect -- score only how much quantified self-scale text is present.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. Who filed the comment -- a large, well-funded trade body versus one grower -- is not visible to a text-only model, but it leaves an unmistakable fingerprint, because large filers state their scale as a matter of house style. R07 recites '1,500 member companies', '$323 billion in annual premiums', '67 percent of homeowners'; R48 (State Farm) recites '40 million active automobile insurance policies' and '19,400 agents'; R11 (UnitedHealth Group) recites '225,000 people' and '125 million people'; R19 (A2LA) recites 'over 3700 actively accredited organizations'; R22 (Center for Biological Diversity) recites '1.7 million members'. The sentence is a status display, not an argument about the rule. Tagged mixed because the same institutional resources plausibly also buy genuine analytic work, so the discounted and undiscounted readouts should bracket it.
proposals.upstream_parent: institutional resources, membership base and market position of the filer

proposals.name: Formal letterhead and professional drafting apparatus
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much formal correspondence apparatus surrounds the substance. Count as extent: a full postal address block for the filer; a named individual addressee with their title and agency mailing address; a structured 'Re:' or 'SUBJECT:' line naming the docket and the rule's full title; a formal salutation ('Dear Ms. X', 'Dear Sir or Madam'); a submission-channel line ('Submitted electronically via www.regulations.gov', 'VIA ELECTRONIC SUBMISSION'); numbered or lettered section headings; footnotes with full source citations; and a closing signature block with the signer's name and job title. Anchors: 0 = none of these, the text simply begins; 5 = salutation plus Re: line plus signature block; 10 = the full apparatus, including addressee title, submission-channel line, headings and footnotes. Do NOT judge whether the formality is appropriate or whether it signals competence -- count only how much of this apparatus is on the page.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. Whether a comment passed through a professional regulatory shop is invisible to a text-only model, but the shop leaves a formatting fingerprint that is fully separable from the argument. R12 (Ice Miller LLP) carries three separate 'WRITER'S DIRECT NUMBER' blocks and a formal 'DESCRIPTION OF ICE MILLER LLP' heading before any analysis; R04 (AbbVie), R15 (Prudential), R38 (Health Benefits Institute) and R60 (Parenteral Drug Association) all carry the complete address-block / Re: line / named-addressee / signature-with-title package. By contrast R13, R18, R21 and R08 begin mid-thought with no apparatus at all. The apparatus is bought, not reasoned; it is also stable across every filing a given office makes. Tagged mixed because paid drafting help plausibly also improves the substance.
proposals.upstream_parent: professional drafting assistance -- in-house regulatory-affairs staff, outside counsel, or a communications department preparing the filing

proposals.name: Roster, masthead and attachment-index filler
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the share of the item that consists of directory-style listing material rather than connected prose. Count: boards of directors and officer rosters with names, companies and cities; multi-office address footers; lists of member or coalition organisations; indexes or manifests of attached files; and batch labels such as '[Batch N of M]'. Score by proportion of the visible text, not by whether the listing is informative. Anchors: 0 = no listing material at all; 3 = a short list of a few signatory organisations; 6 = roughly a third of the text is roster or index material; 10 = the item is essentially a roster or a file manifest with only a sentence or two of prose. Do NOT judge whether the listed affiliations are prestigious and do NOT treat listing material as padding or as credibility -- score its extent only.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. Only an established organisation has a forty-name board printed on its letterhead or the staff capacity to file eighteen batches of attachments, and that unseen fact leaves a large, easily learned block of text. R29 is roughly three-quarters Georgia Agribusiness Council board roster ('STEVE CROUCH, Newton Crouch Inc, Griffin, GA' and dozens more) before two paragraphs on thiamethoxam; R44 is a pure index of PDF filenames ('BTS - Household Cost of Transportation.pdf', 'ALA - Ozone.pdf') with no argument at all; R60 lists officers and thirteen directors before the letter; R10 lists every member district and city of the Calleguas Creek stakeholder group; R05 carries a four-office national/California/Pacific-Northwest/Hawaii address footer. None of this text argues anything about the rule. Tagged mixed because organisational maturity plausibly also produces better substantive comment.
proposals.upstream_parent: organisational formality and age -- established bodies with governance structures, branded letterhead, and staff to assemble large multi-file submissions

proposals.name: Verbatim mirroring of the agency's own notice language
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much of the comment restates the agency's notice back to the agency before or instead of saying anything of the filer's own. Count paragraphs that recapitulate: the date and Federal Register citation of the notice, its stated purpose, the design of the study or collection being proposed, the statutory authority behind it, and the agency's own list of questions -- reproduced in the agency's own vocabulary and sentence shapes. Anchors: 0 = the comment never restates the notice; 3 = one sentence identifying what is being commented on; 6 = a full paragraph of recapitulation; 10 = half or more of the text is restatement of the notice, with only a small original remainder. Do NOT judge whether the restatement is accurate or whether framing the issue is helpful -- score only how much mirrored notice-language is present.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. Repeat filers work from a skeleton whose opening third is a mechanical restatement of whatever notice is being answered; the fingerprint is text that is fluent, on-topic, docket-specific and yet entirely derivative. Three letters from the same office appear in this slice -- R07, R27 and R55 (NAMIC) -- and each opens with a near-identical structure: date of publication, what the notice requests, then the same verbatim self-description paragraph, with the original contribution deferred. R31 (Covered California) and R20 (Center for Auto Safety) similarly recapitulate the notice's framing at length. Because the mirrored text is copied from the agency, it is guaranteed to look topically apt to any text model while carrying none of the filer's own thinking. Tagged not-mixed: reproducing the agency's own words is not itself a contribution, even when the office that reproduces them also contributes elsewhere.
proposals.upstream_parent: template reuse by a repeat-filing regulatory-affairs office that produces many near-identical letters from one skeleton

proposals.name: First-person credential and tenure recitation
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which an individual writer describes their own qualifications, occupation, tenure or personal stake before or while commenting. Count: licences, certificates and ratings; degrees; job titles and employers; board or committee membership; years of experience or hours logged; and first-hand-experience framing ('I have fished these waters for thirty years', 'as someone who was an at-risk student'). Anchors: 0 = no self-description of the writer at all; 3 = a bare name or one-clause role mention; 6 = a sentence or two of credentials; 10 = a full paragraph enumerating licences, degrees, positions and years. Do NOT assess whether the credentials are genuine, relevant, or sufficient, and do NOT treat an uncredentialed writer as less serious -- score only how much credential text is present.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. Seniority and occupational position are unobservable to a text-only model, but individual commenters routinely announce them, so the factor leaves a crisp trace. R17 opens with 'A&P/IA, Com, Inst, ME' and then unpacks it across a paragraph -- FAA mechanic with Inspection Authorization, private pilot, Bachelor's in Aeronautical Engineering, Master's in Electrical Engineering, 'over 6000 hours flying experience'. R50 opens 'I have fished recreationally for Black Sea Bass ... for over 30 years and have a degree in Marine Biology'. R45 opens 'I currently serve on the board for the NWPB. I am the sales and marketing director for Leger and Son, Inc.'. R51 opens with an at-risk-student and grant-administration biography. The recitation is a status move that is separable from the argument that follows -- R45's actual comment is two sentences of generic endorsement. Tagged mixed because real expertise plausibly does improve the substance that follows.
proposals.upstream_parent: the author's professional standing, seniority and personal stake in the docket

proposals.name: Advocacy-campaign petition register
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the comment reads in the register of an organised advocacy campaign's supporter template rather than an independently composed submission. Count as extent: second-person imperative petitioning ('please act swiftly', 'I urge you to', 'we urge the agency to take NO action'); urgency and stakes superlatives ('there's no time to waste', 'for future generations', 'must be protected, not disrupted and destroyed'); round-number statistics presented without citation; named political figures used as antagonists; generic framing that would fit many dockets rather than this one; and a visible seam where fluent templated paragraphs are followed by looser personal writing in a different voice. Anchors: 0 = none of this register; 5 = clearly petition-flavoured but docket-specific; 10 = the whole item is campaign-template prose, or template prose plus a personal postscript. Do NOT judge whether the position taken is right, whether the passion is sincere, or whether templated comment is legitimate -- score only how much of this register is present.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. Whether text was drafted by a campaign and forwarded by a supporter is unobservable, but the pipeline leaves several traces at once: uniform petition phrasing, uncited round statistics, and sometimes the email envelope itself. R06 is textbook supplied text -- 'I respectfully ask that you please help protect the Banggai Cardinalfish', 'declined by up to 90%', 'About 75% to 80% of individuals collected from the wild die', closing with 'There's no time to waste. Please act swiftly.' R53 is visibly an email-campaign body ('I strongly oppose President Donald Trump and EPA Administrator Andrew Wheeler's attack ...') carried in with its mail headers and then trailing off into a rambling first-person postscript about nuclear power -- the template/personal seam in one document. R40 ('I applaud HHS ... However, I encourage HHS to go even further') and R13 ('It must be protected, not disrupted and destroyed ... not just a few!') carry the same register. Tagged mixed because campaign staff can and do write accurate substantive claims into their templates.
proposals.upstream_parent: advocacy-organisation campaign infrastructure (supplied text, action alerts, and email-to-docket pipelines that route many similar submissions into the record)

proposals.name: Rule-specific engagement vs. organizational self-promotion
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the comment's content directly analyzes or engages the specific rule, provision, or agency request, versus describing the submitting organization's own size, mission, membership, or credentials. A 10 means the letter devotes the substantial majority of its text to specific analysis of the rule's provisions, with organizational description limited to a brief identifying sentence. A 0 means the letter is dominated by paragraphs describing the organization's membership counts, mission statement, and market share, with little or no specific analysis of the rule's actual provisions.
proposals.rationale: R14 and R51 (both National Association of Mutual Insurance Companies letters) spend most of their visible text reciting NAMIC's membership size and market share before reaching only a thin, generic reaction to the collection request; both are dense_high_card_low. By contrast R37 (South Carolina DHEC) opens briefly then moves immediately into specific critique of the proposed rule's reporting-threshold language. This ratio plausibly explains why the dense model rates institutionally-padded letters high while a criterion-based scorer, forced to find rule-specific substance, rates them low.

proposals.name: Quantification of real-world stakes or impact
proposals.instruction: Score the degree to which the comment supplies specific, checkable figures (dollar amounts, populations affected, physical quantities, percentages, casualty/injury counts, historical baselines) that let the reader gauge the magnitude of the rule's consequences. A 10 gives multiple specific, well-attributed figures tied directly to the argument. A 0 offers only vague qualitative claims ('a lot,' 'many,' 'significant harm') with no quantification at all.
proposals.rationale: R45 (Truck Safety Coalition) anchors its argument in specific figures -- 5,700 deaths, 155,000 injuries, $66 billion in losses, a 71% increase since 2009 -- and R47 (American Samoa DMWR) sets the proposed 13,000-lb catch limit against a documented 21,139-lb five-year historical average. Both are dense_high_card_low, suggesting the dense model rewards this kind of checkable quantification in a way the scorecard's bank currently does not fully capture.

proposals.name: Pinpoint citation to the specific provision under comment
proposals.instruction: Score whether the comment identifies and engages the exact provision, page, paragraph, or sentence of the proposed rule it is responding to (by quotation, section number, or direct pin-cite), as opposed to discussing the general topic area without locating its argument in the rule's actual text. A 10 quotes or precisely pin-cites the specific language at issue. A 0 never identifies which specific part of the proposal it is addressing.
proposals.rationale: R12 links each of its three pointed questions to a specific paragraph of the Federal Register notice (e.g., 'p-13', 'p-24') despite being very short overall; R18 quotes the exact text of 14 CFR 91.107(a)(3) and proposes a specific redline. Both are dense_low_card_high, suggesting the scorecard rewards this kind of pinpoint textual engagement more than the dense model does.

proposals.name: Topical focus and freedom from digression
proposals.instruction: Score how tightly the comment stays on the docket's actual subject matter throughout its full length. A 10 stays entirely on-topic from first sentence to last. A 0 wanders into extended tangents, unrelated statutes, or personal asides that have no clear connection to the rule under comment.
proposals.rationale: R32 drifts from wildfire smoke chemistry into the Equal Access to Justice Act, tribal forest law, and general anti-litigation commentary; R50 pivots from opposing a methane rule into an extended personal meditation on nuclear energy and 'tree hugging.' Both are dense_high_card_low (dense_pct .741 and .921 respectively), a striking pattern given how unfocused the comments are -- this criterion tests whether the dense model is rewarding raw length or topic-adjacent engagement over actual focus.

proposals.name: Original firsthand text vs. formulaic template language
proposals.instruction: Score whether the comment's language is specific to this commenter's own situation and this particular docket, versus reading like a generic template that could be dropped into many different comment periods with minor edits. A 10 is clearly composed for this specific submission with situation-specific detail. A 0 reads as boilerplate (e.g., a generic extension-request form) with the docket number as the only customized element.
proposals.rationale: R15, R24, R40, and R49 are all comment-period extension requests that follow a near-identical template (trade association credentials, complexity claim, requested number of days) -- all four are dense_low_card_high, suggesting the scorecard rewards this formulaic genre more than the dense model does, which may be picking up on its generic, reusable phrasing.

proposals.name: Disclosed firsthand expertise grounding the claims
proposals.instruction: Score whether the commenter explicitly establishes personal, verifiable firsthand expertise or direct experience (credentials, years of hands-on practice, direct observation) that specifically grounds the technical claims made, as opposed to speaking from unstated or purely institutional authority. A 10 clearly discloses relevant credentials or experience that directly support the specific claims made. A 0 offers no such grounding -- claims stand on their own or on unstated authority.
proposals.rationale: R03 opens by listing the commenter's A&P/IA mechanic certification, engineering degrees, and 6,000+ flight hours before making detailed technical claims about ELT failure rates; R19 grounds a fisheries argument in 30 years of firsthand charter fishing and a marine biology degree. Both are dense_low_card_high (R03 dense_pct .095, R19 dense_pct .164) despite the depth of disclosed expertise, suggesting the scorecard credits this kind of grounding more than the dense model does.

proposals.name: Specific actionable recommendation or proposed rule text
proposals.instruction: Score whether the comment proposes a concrete, specific action, threshold, or alternative rule text for the agency to adopt, as opposed to stating only agreement, disagreement, or support/opposition with no proposed specifics. A 10 proposes exact alternative language, a specific number, or an unambiguous concrete action. A 0 states only a general position (e.g., 'we support this' or 'we oppose this') with nothing specific attached.
proposals.rationale: R18 proposes an exact redline to 14 CFR 91.107(a)(3); R33 requests a specific compliance-time change (60 months instead of 24) tied to a named part number. By contrast R08 ('we support that adjustment of fees') and R23 ('UAL concurs... and have no further comments') state only a bare position -- and R08/R23 are both dense_high_card_low, showing the dense model does not appear to penalize the absence of any specific ask the way a scorecard focused on this dimension would.

proposals.name: Technical precision achieved concisely (technical economy)
proposals.instruction: Score the comment for combining (a) concrete, verifiable technical detail -- part numbers, dates, thresholds, section numbers -- with (b) brevity: no unnecessary padding, throat-clearing, or repetition. A 10 conveys precise technical content in the fewest words needed. A 0 either lacks technical precision, or buries whatever precision exists under substantial unrelated or repetitive padding.
proposals.rationale: R39 (International Aero Engines) makes a precise, three-sentence technical request naming exact engine model numbers and a specific service bulletin; R33 (Japan Airlines) does the same in two sentences. Both are short and dense_low_card_high. By contrast R32 and R50 are long, repetitive, and technically imprecise despite being dense_high_card_low -- the interaction of precision AND concision appears to run opposite to how the two scores rank these rows.

proposals.name: Argument-carried weight vs. appeal to institutional size
proposals.instruction: Score whether the comment's persuasive force rests on the substance of its reasoning and evidence, as opposed to resting on an implicit appeal to the submitting organization's size, membership count, or market share (e.g., citing '1,500 member companies' or '225,000 employees' as if that were itself the argument). A 10 relies entirely on reasoned, evidence-based argument. A 0 substitutes recitation of organizational scale or authority for actual argument.
proposals.rationale: R14, R17, R20, and R51 (NAMIC and State Farm letters) each open with statistics about membership size, market share, or policy counts (e.g., 'more than 1,500... member companies,' 'over 40 million active automobile insurance policies') as the primary credential-establishing move before offering comparatively thin substantive analysis. All four are dense_high_card_low, suggesting the dense model may be responsive to this authority signal in a way a criteria-based scorer is not.

proposals.name: Direct responsiveness to the agency's own enumerated questions
proposals.instruction: For comments responding to a notice that poses specific numbered or itemized questions, score whether the comment explicitly answers those specific questions in the order or structure the agency posed them, versus offering unstructured general remarks that ignore the notice's actual question structure. A 10 explicitly walks through and answers the agency's specific questions. A 0 ignores the notice's question structure entirely.
proposals.rationale: R09 (AbbVie) explicitly numbers its response to FDA's stated questions ('1. Whether the proposed collection... 3. Ways to enhance the quality...'), directly mirroring the notice's own enumeration; R54 (Center for Food Safety) similarly organizes its response around 'the areas posed by the Agency.' This structured responsiveness is a distinct, checkable property from generic on-topic-ness and may be under- or over-weighted differently by the two scoring approaches.

proposals.name: Internal logical coherence of the presented argument
proposals.instruction: Score whether the comment's reasoning proceeds coherently from stated premises to a clear conclusion, without unexplained gaps, self-contradictions, or non-sequiturs, as the text is actually presented to the reader. A 10 is fully coherent and easy to follow start to finish. A 0 contains major structural breaks (e.g., a numbered list whose items are missing) or leaps between unrelated claims with no connecting logic.
proposals.rationale: R48's numbered demand list runs '1. 2. 4. 5. 6. 7. 8.' with items 1-3 apparently missing their text before the demands resume in paragraph form, leaving the structure broken as presented; R50 leaps from opposing a methane rule to an unconnected personal reflection on nuclear energy without a transition. Both are notable outliers, and this criterion targets whether such breaks are being priced into either score.

proposals.name: Developed argumentative prose vs. list or index of attachments
proposals.instruction: Score whether the submitted text itself contains developed explanatory or argumentative prose about the rule, as opposed to being substantially a list, table of contents, index of exhibits, or citation list with no accompanying analysis in the text itself. A 10 is entirely developed prose making a case. A 0 is essentially just a list of document or file names with no argumentative content.
proposals.rationale: R60 is literally a 'MASTER INDEX' of attachment filenames (PDFs and spreadsheets) submitted as one batch of a joint comment, with no argumentative prose of its own in the visible text -- yet it is dense_high_card_low with a very high dense_pct of .942. This is a strong candidate for a criterion the scorecard may already implicitly capture (via low content scores) but that this slice suggests the dense model is missing.

proposals.name: New information added beyond registering a bare position
proposals.instruction: Score how much new information, data, analysis, or reasoning the comment gives the agency to work with, beyond simply registering agreement or disagreement. A 10 supplies substantial new information, data, or analysis useful to the agency's decision. A 0 supplies nothing beyond a bare 'we agree' / 'we disagree' with no supporting content.
proposals.rationale: R23 ('UAL concurs with the proposed rule and have no further comments') and R46 ('Concur, no additional comments will be forthcoming') add no information beyond registering agreement, yet both are dense_high_card_low with very high dense_pct (.898 and .947). By contrast R47 supplies specific catch-rate data the agency did not already have. This dimension -- informational contribution, independent of position or tone -- looks like a clean source of the disagreement between the two scores.

proposals.name: Historical or precedential grounding of the request
proposals.instruction: Score whether the comment situates its position within relevant regulatory history, prior agency actions, or precedent (e.g., citing how the agency handled comparable past dockets, or tracing the issue's history over time), as opposed to treating the current proposal in isolation with no historical context. A 10 explicitly and specifically grounds the argument in comparable precedent or history. A 0 offers no historical or precedential context at all.
proposals.rationale: R40 (Al Fakher Tobacco) cites two specific prior ANPRM comment-period extensions (menthol, Docket FDA-2013-N-0521; NNN, Docket FDA-2016-N-2527) with exact day counts as precedent for its own request; R45 (Truck Safety Coalition) traces the agency's awareness of side-underride risk back to a specific 1969 statement, spanning over 50 years of inaction. Both ground otherwise simple requests in specific historical precedent, a property the current criteria set may not isolate.

proposals.name: Technical substantiation vs. ideological/emotional characterization
proposals.instruction: Score whether the comment's persuasive force rests on specific technical, factual, or legal substantiation, as opposed to resting primarily on ideological or emotionally loaded characterization (e.g., labeling a prior rule an 'attack,' 'illegal,' or a 'War on Coal') without corresponding technical detail to back the characterization. A 10 backs every strong characterization with specific technical or factual support. A 0 relies on charged rhetoric with little or no technical substantiation behind it.
proposals.rationale: R11 (Murray Energy) characterizes the prior rule as a 'woefully misguided and irrational attack,' an 'illegal de facto ban,' and part of a 'War on Coal' -- strong rhetoric with comparatively little specific technical rebuttal in the visible text -- and is dense_high_card_low (dense_pct .826). By contrast R37 and R42 disagree just as forcefully with agency positions but do so through specific statutory citations and point-by-point technical rebuttal, suggesting rhetorical intensity untethered from substantiation may be something the dense model rewards that a criteria bank would not.

proposals.name: Transmittal boilerplate share of visible text
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much of this comment's visible text consists of generic transmittal/cover-letter boilerplate (e.g., 'please see attached', 'thank you for the opportunity to comment', formulaic salutations and closings) rather than argument specific to this docket. 0 = no boilerplate, all substantive text; 10 = almost entirely boilerplate. Do not judge whether the boilerplate is appropriate, polite, or well-written -- score only how much of it is present.
proposals.rationale: R01 opens with a pure transmittal sentence ('Please find attached comments...Thank you for the opportunity to provide comment') before any substance; R27 (Boeing) is almost entirely the boilerplate line 'Concur, no additional comments will be forthcoming.' This transmittal framing is a stylistic habit of frequent-filer organizations, not a mark of argument quality.

proposals.name: Letterhead / contact-metadata density
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much of the visible text is occupied by letterhead/contact-metadata elements (mailing addresses, phone/fax numbers, websites, lists of officers/directors/board members) rather than the body of the comment itself. 0 = no such elements; 10 = the letterhead/roster dominates the visible text. Do not judge whether the organization is legitimate or prestigious -- score only the extent of this formatting element.
proposals.rationale: R02 (PDA) carries a full letterhead with a twelve-person officer/director roster and two international addresses before the letter body; R10 (Georgia Agribusiness Council) is dominated by a multi-page board-of-directors list. Neither roster bears on the substance of the comment.

proposals.name: OCR scan-extraction artifact density
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the visible text shows signs of OCR/scan extraction artifacts -- garbled characters, broken or fused words, misrendered symbols, misaligned columns -- consistent with a scanned or faxed document run through optical character recognition. 0 = clean, extraction-error-free text; 10 = pervasive garbling throughout. Do not judge the quality of the argument being made -- score only the extent of extraction noise.
proposals.rationale: R10's board roster is heavily OCR-garbled ('Chairm~n', fused address fragments like '~:~~~~~~~r'e~'B'$:'); R13 (UPS Airlines) is so badly scanned that words fuse and drop letters ('lowe e023 ups', 'Simple FOD checks' rendered as broken fragments). This is an artifact of the source scan, not of the argument's substance.

proposals.name: Numbered-list / enumerated-comment structure
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the comment is organized as an explicit numbered or enumerated list of discrete points (e.g., '1.', '2.', 'Comment #1 of 10', a repeated table template per point) as opposed to free-flowing prose. 0 = no enumerated structure; 10 = the entire comment is presented as a numbered/tabular list. Do not judge whether the enumerated points are individually good or well-reasoned -- score only the extent of this structural device.
proposals.rationale: R03 (AIA) structures its ten points as a repeated 'Comment # of 10' table template; R24 (International Aero Engines) presents its request as a short list of specific engine-model corrections. The enumerated form is a drafting convention, independent of whether the underlying points are correct.

proposals.name: Attachment-index / cover-page share of text
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much of the visible text functions as an index, cover page, or file-list pointing to separately attached material (e.g., filenames, 'Batch X of Y', 'See attached file(s)' immediately followed by a list of exhibit titles) rather than being the substantive comment itself. 0 = the visible text is entirely the substantive comment; 10 = the visible text is entirely an index/cover page for unseen attachments. Do not judge the value of the attachments themselves -- score only how much of the visible text is index/cover material.
proposals.rationale: R04 (NRDC et al.) is literally a '[Batch 9 of 18]' master index of attachment filenames with no argument of its own; R16 and R23 both open with 'See attached file(s)' before the real letter begins, meaning part of the visible text is a pure attachment-pointer rather than comment.

proposals.name: Organizational scale self-description
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how explicitly the text states the submitting organization's scale or resources -- e.g., a specific membership count, revenue figure, market-share percentage, or employee/customer count. 0 = no such scale statement anywhere in the text; 10 = the text prominently and repeatedly quantifies the organization's size. Do not judge whether the organization's size makes its argument more or less correct -- score only whether such a scale statement is present in the text.
proposals.rationale: R22 and R51 (NAMIC) both state '1,500 member companies... $323 billion in annual premiums / 55 percent of the auto market'; R39 (UnitedHealth Group) states 'workforce of 225,000 people... 125 million people worldwide.' These scale claims are about the filer's resources, not the argument's merits, though a well-resourced filer may also genuinely produce more careful comments, which is why this is tagged mixed.

proposals.name: Reusable form-letter self-description phrasing
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much a passage in this comment reads like a reusable, pre-drafted 'about us' paragraph -- generic organizational self-description phrasing that could plausibly be pasted verbatim into many different comment letters from the same submitter with only the docket-specific details changed. 0 = all text reads as bespoke to this specific docket; 10 = a substantial passage reads as interchangeable boilerplate reused across filings. Do not judge whether the self-description is accurate or the organization credible -- score only how 'reusable' the phrasing appears.
proposals.rationale: R22, R38, and R51 are three separate NAMIC filings (different dockets, different years) that carry essentially the same 'NAMIC is the largest property/casualty insurance trade group... 55 percent of the auto market' paragraph almost verbatim, indicating a stock paragraph reused across submissions rather than bespoke drafting for each docket.

proposals.name: Legal/regulatory citation apparatus density
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the text displays formal legal/regulatory citation apparatus -- numbered footnotes, pincites to the Federal Register/CFR/U.S.C., precise docket/RIN number recitation, or law-firm-style formal phrasing ('the undersigned', 'respectfully submits'). 0 = no such apparatus; 10 = dense, brief-style citation apparatus throughout. Do not judge whether the legal argument itself is correct -- score only the extent of this citation/formality apparatus.
proposals.rationale: R31 (Ice Miller LLP) cites specific Treasury regulation subsections with case-style precision (e.g., '1.457-12(e)(2)(i)'); R35, R42, and R46 (extension-request letters from AFFI, ACC, and Consumer Brands) all carry footnoted Federal Register pincites. This apparatus signals professional/legal drafting support, which could reflect both a nuisance halo effect and genuinely more careful argumentation, hence mixed.

proposals.name: Comment-period timing/procedural request share
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much of this comment is a procedural request about timing (e.g., asking to extend the comment period) or an explicit statement about time pressure (e.g., referencing a holiday season or insufficient time to prepare), as opposed to comment on the substance of the proposed rule. 0 = entirely substantive comment on the rule, no timing/procedural content; 10 = the comment is entirely a timing/procedural request. Do not judge whether the timing request is reasonable or justified -- score only how much of the text is devoted to it.
proposals.rationale: R35 (AFFI), R42 (ACC), R45 (PMI), and R46 (Consumer Brands) are each entirely a request to extend the comment period -- R42 explicitly invokes 'just after the Holiday Season' as its justification. None of the four engages the substance of the proposed rule at all; a criterion-based scorecard could easily reward the mere presence of a well-formed, on-topic procedural ask, while a reader looking for substantive engagement would not.

proposals.name: Author professional title/seniority in signature
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how explicitly the visible signature block attaches a formal professional title to the named author (e.g., 'Senior Manager', 'Vice President', 'President and CEO', 'Director', a named regulatory-affairs department). 0 = no name/title given, or an anonymous/untitled individual; 10 = a fully elaborated senior title and department are given. Do not judge whether the title reflects genuine expertise -- score only whether such a title is stated in the text.
proposals.rationale: R01 signs off as 'Cameron Harsh, Senior Manager, Organic & Animal Policy, Center for Food Safety' and R40 (AbbVie) closes with a titled 'Regulatory Policy and Intelligence' office block, whereas R09, R11, and R56 are anonymous individual commenters with no title or affiliation at all. The presence of a senior title is a signature-block artifact that may or may not track the actual expertise behind the argument, hence mixed.

proposals.name: Provision-Level Anchoring
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when claims are repeatedly tied to specific provisions, paragraphs, forms, standards, or proposed text and their practical meaning; score 0 when the comment offers only broad policy assertions without textual anchors.
proposals.rationale: R16 analyzes specific Renewable Fuel Standard provisions and regulatory language, while R55 identifies exact form boxes and discrepancies between proposed text and instructions.

proposals.name: Mechanistic Causal Explanation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment explains a concrete causal chain from the proposed requirement to operational, safety, economic, or environmental effects; score 0 when it merely asserts that a proposal is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: R05 explains how stretcher mounts and unsecured equipment become crash hazards, and R26 explains why closing federal waters would not address nearshore fishing while affecting subsistence and cultural practices.

proposals.name: Evidence Calibration
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment distinguishes observed facts, estimates, anecdotes, uncertainty, and unanswered questions, and connects evidence to its claims; score 0 when unsupported assertions are presented as settled facts.
proposals.rationale: R03 distinguishes ELT models and asks for comparative failure-rate evidence, while R54 quantifies crashes and fatalities, cites sources, and discusses likely undercounting.

proposals.name: Counterargument Engagement
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment identifies a plausible opposing rationale or agency concern and directly explains why the evidence does or does not support it; score 0 when it ignores contrary considerations.
proposals.rationale: R13 addresses the agency’s rationale for allowing two standards and explains the resulting confusion, while R26 responds directly to the stock-assessment and closure rationale.

proposals.name: Feasible Remedy Design
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment proposes a concrete alternative that could be implemented, with enough technical detail to identify what would change and why; score 0 when it only states a preferred position.
proposals.rationale: R32 specifies the engine models to retain and remove and links that change to a service bulletin, while R36 proposes component-level compliance and explains how aircraft-level requirements create compliance problems.

proposals.name: Applicability Boundaries
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment precisely identifies which products, units, populations, or circumstances are affected and which are not, with a reason for the distinction; score 0 when it treats materially different cases as interchangeable.
proposals.rationale: R29 identifies the precise affected components absent from FedEx’s fleet, while R57 distinguishes overlapping actuator requirements and compliance periods.

proposals.name: Distributional Impact Analysis
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment examines how effects differ across multiple affected groups, especially vulnerable, geographically distinct, or less represented groups; score 0 when impacts are described only for the commenter.
proposals.rationale: R17 discusses drivers across ages and experience levels, R26 addresses fishermen’s subsistence and cultural needs, and R54 quantifies consequences for passenger-vehicle occupants.

proposals.name: Issue-Relevant Representation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the commenter’s role or represented population is clearly connected to the issue and supplies relevant knowledge, constraints, or observations; score 0 when organizational size, credentials, or membership numbers are offered without issue-specific relevance.
proposals.rationale: R05 connects Louisiana’s EMS system and practitioner population to ambulance-safety constraints, while R25 connects insurer market coverage to crash-data collection and its intended uses.

proposals.name: Informational Increment
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment adds concrete facts, analysis, examples, or questions that materially expand understanding of the issue; score 0 when it mainly repeats support or opposition, credentials, courtesy, or a procedural request.
proposals.rationale: R11, R28, and R30 primarily request more time and describe comment-period complexity, whereas R37 adds specific product-safety concerns and detailed regulatory demands.

proposals.name: Substantive Prompt Coverage
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment addresses multiple substantive questions or distinct elements raised by the agency and gives issue-specific responses; score 0 when it addresses only process, timing, or a general position.
proposals.rationale: R08 responds to several best-practice topics in the agency’s guidance request, and R41 supplies ten structured comments on specific special conditions; R15 and R46 mainly request extensions.

proposals.name: Diagnosis-to-Remedy Coherence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the factual diagnosis, identified problem, proposed remedy, and claimed justification form a consistent chain; score 0 when recommendations are disconnected, contradictory, or unrelated to the stated problem.
proposals.rationale: R16 connects fuel-program provisions, industry operations, and requested regulatory changes, while R05 consistently links each funding request to a specific ambulance-safety hazard.

proposals.name: Verification and Enforcement Design
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment specifies how compliance, performance, or claimed effects should be tested, documented, monitored, or enforced; score 0 when it demands action without any means of verification.
proposals.rationale: R07 asks what failure tests and documentation should establish acceptable airflow behavior, while R37 requests inspections, spot testing, and escalating enforcement mechanisms.

proposals.name: Transition and Interaction Awareness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment analyzes timing, grandfathering, overlapping requirements, existing obligations, or interactions with related rules and explains their practical consequences; score 0 when it treats the proposal as isolated from existing requirements.
proposals.rationale: R32 compares the proposed applicability list with an existing service bulletin, R36 discusses overlapping fleet and component requirements, and R57 compares compliance periods across related actions.

proposals.name: Public-Interest Balance
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment candidly states the commenter’s interests while also weighing effects on consumers, communities, competitors, public resources, or other stakeholders; score 0 when private benefit is presented as sufficient justification.
proposals.rationale: R06 acknowledges imported-produce interests while discussing barriers to entry and regulatory purpose, and R24 combines coal-industry concerns with effects on workers, electricity customers, states, and vulnerable households.

proposals.name: Substantive Density
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when nearly every paragraph advances issue-specific facts, reasoning, or recommendations; score 0 when most of the text consists of headers, credentials, organizational boilerplate, procedural filler, or rhetoric.
proposals.rationale: R11, R28, and R30 contain substantial procedural and institutional framing with little issue analysis, while R54 and R56 use dense text to supply statistics, mechanisms, and concrete regulatory proposals.

proposals.name: Institutional scale cues
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the text displays organizational size, membership counts, geographic reach, official letterhead, or institutional prominence; do not judge whether this feature is good.
proposals.rationale: These visible status cues may influence how institutional submissions are processed or interpreted without constituting substantive reasoning. They appear in R08, R15, R30, R38, and R50.

proposals.name: Personal credential display
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the author states personal credentials, office, seniority, licenses, education, tenure, or direct experience; do not judge whether the credentials are valuable.
proposals.rationale: Self-presented credentials can affect perceived authority while also sometimes reflecting genuine subject knowledge, making this a mixed nuisance. Examples include R21, R45, and R55.

proposals.name: Professional legal drafting
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the text uses lawyerly drafting conventions, formal legal framing, structured sections, defined terms, or counsel attribution; do not judge whether the drafting is good.
proposals.rationale: Access to counsel or professional editors leaves recognizable drafting fingerprints that may affect reception independently of the underlying substance, while also potentially improving substance. Examples include R11, R33, R35, and R56.

proposals.name: Submission packaging
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the item contains cover messages, attachment references, master indexes, duplicate versions, transmittal language, or other submission-production artifacts; do not judge whether the package is effective.
proposals.rationale: Administrative production practices can create text signals unrelated to the comment's substantive content. They are visible in R09, R27, R39, R46, and R60.

proposals.name: Citation apparatus
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the text contains footnotes, Federal Register citations, statutes, studies, URLs, cross-references, or bibliographic detail; do not judge the accuracy or usefulness of the citations.
proposals.rationale: Citation density can act as a proxy for organizational research capacity or drafting convention rather than the actual force of the reasoning, though those resources may also support genuine substance. Examples include R05, R23, R32, and R42.

proposals.name: Technical identifier density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the text uses specialized acronyms, model numbers, part numbers, docket identifiers, standards codes, or regulatory alphanumeric strings; do not judge whether the technical detail is correct.
proposals.rationale: Identifier-heavy language may reflect topic, industry convention, or author specialization and can influence text processing independently of substantive quality. Examples include R20, R40, R45, and R59.

proposals.name: Procedural template language
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the text uses standardized phrases requesting extensions, acknowledging opportunities, stating support, or directing the agency to an attachment; do not judge whether the request is appropriate.
proposals.rationale: Repeated procedural boilerplate can arise from workflow templates and submission norms without indicating the merits of the comment. Examples include R06, R17, R36, R49, and R54.

proposals.name: Mobilization and identity language
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the text uses collective identity, moral appeals, emotional urgency, religious language, activist slogans, or community-specific framing; do not judge whether the appeals are persuasive or justified.
proposals.rationale: Campaign or community communication styles can systematically shape wording while being separate from substantive analysis. Examples include R07, R12, R41, R43, and R48.

proposals.name: OCR and layout corruption
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the text shows scanning artifacts, character substitutions, broken spacing, malformed symbols, page remnants, or degraded formatting; do not judge whether the underlying comment is good.
proposals.rationale: Production and ingestion pipelines can leave noisy textual traces that affect automated reading without changing the author's substantive position. Examples include R12, R26, R37, and R59.

proposals.name: Timing and urgency markers
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the text explicitly mentions deadlines, delayed responses, holiday timing, requests for expedited action, or limited preparation time; do not judge whether the timing claim is valid.
proposals.rationale: Timing circumstances can alter the visible framing and may also affect how much preparation was possible, so the channel should be treated as a sensitivity band. Examples include R06, R17, R44, and R49.

proposals.name: Rule-text anchoring
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment identifies precise proposed provisions, definitions, paragraphs, or requirements and analyzes them; score 0 when it discusses only the topic generally without locating the issue in the text.
proposals.rationale: The detailed provision-level analysis in R04 and R11 contrasts with broad statements in R01 and R14.

proposals.name: Actionable drafting
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment supplies concrete replacement language, fields, thresholds, procedures, or other text an agency could implement; score 0 when it offers only approval, opposition, or an abstract request.
proposals.rationale: R29 proposes exact regulatory language, and R34 supplies structured replacement text, while R31 and R59 largely express general preferences.

proposals.name: Mechanism-to-effect reasoning
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment explains a plausible chain from the proposed provision through an operational mechanism to a specific consequence; score 0 when it merely asserts that the proposal is good or harmful.
proposals.rationale: R09 connects federal and nearshore closures to fishing impacts, and R32 explains how unsecured ambulance equipment becomes dangerous projectiles.

proposals.name: Traceable empirical support
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when important factual claims are supported by specific measurements, records, studies, dates, comparisons, or identifiable sources; score 0 when factual claims are unsupported generalizations.
proposals.rationale: R47 provides crash counts, injury estimates, historical evidence, and citations, while R28 and R52 make many broad claims with limited traceable support.

proposals.name: Technical domain application
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when specialized knowledge is applied directly to the docket issue through technically relevant facts or analysis; score 0 when credentials or domain labels appear without issue-specific application.
proposals.rationale: R50 applies aircraft-maintenance and engineering experience to failure rates and redundant inspections, while R07 and R33 foreground experience or organizational status more than technical analysis.

proposals.name: Counterargument engagement
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment identifies plausible objections, competing evidence, or agency assumptions and answers them explicitly; score 0 when it presents only one-sided advocacy.
proposals.rationale: R04 discusses acceptable transient airflow reversal and alternative testing risks, and R37 addresses historical-range concerns and conservation tradeoffs.

proposals.name: Alternative comparison
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment compares the requested approach with feasible alternatives using explicit criteria such as effectiveness, burden, risk, or consistency; score 0 when no alternative is considered.
proposals.rationale: R12 compares size limits with bag limits, and R11 compares multiple ways to report unknown amounts.

proposals.name: Implementation feasibility
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment addresses who would implement the proposal, required systems or resources, compliance steps, and practical constraints; score 0 when the recommendation has no implementation analysis.
proposals.rationale: R04 discusses testing, maintenance, controls, and documentation, while R13 and R60 request streamlined or expanded policies without explaining implementation.

proposals.name: Scope precision
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment carefully identifies the affected entities, components, populations, cases, or time period and avoids overbroad application; score 0 when its request is untargeted or its scope is unclear.
proposals.rationale: R03 identifies specific engine components absent from the commenter’s fleet, and R58 narrows applicability to the engine models actually implicated.

proposals.name: Cross-document coherence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment reconciles the proposal with related rules, standards, forms, guidance, service bulletins, or prior requirements and identifies inconsistencies; score 0 when relevant surrounding authorities are ignored.
proposals.rationale: R11 compares the proposed rule with form instructions and statutory language, while R30 and R55 identify conflicts among overlapping airworthiness directives and bulletins.

proposals.name: Uncertainty calibration
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment distinguishes established facts, inferences, unknowns, and needed evidence and proposes how uncertainty could be resolved; score 0 when speculation is presented as certainty.
proposals.rationale: R02 questions whether the proposed sample can answer the research question, and R50 asks for missing failure-rate comparisons rather than assuming them.

proposals.name: Consequences across stakeholders
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment identifies concrete effects on multiple affected groups or systems, including burdens, benefits, distributional effects, or unintended consequences; score 0 when consequences are asserted only for the commenter’s preferred interest.
proposals.rationale: R09 considers fishermen, cultural practices, territorial waters, and stock management, while R32 considers EMS practitioners, patients, equipment, and crash safety.

proposals.name: Decision-relevant prioritization
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment ranks problems, states conditions or thresholds, and makes clear which changes are essential versus optional; score 0 when numerous requests are presented without priority or decision logic.
proposals.rationale: R37 distinguishes last-resort range expansion from native-range conservation, and R54 specifies multiple regulatory demands with inspection and enforcement priorities.

proposals.name: Focused issue coverage
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment remains tightly organized around the docket’s actual question while developing the relevant issue in depth; score 0 when it is mostly generic, tangential, or directed at unrelated grievances.
proposals.rationale: R23 focuses its analysis on the age-range design of a specific driver study, whereas R52 and R28 mix the docket issue with numerous loosely connected topics.

proposals.name: Agency-question responsiveness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment directly answers the agency’s stated questions or evaluation criteria with docket-specific reasoning; score 0 when it merely signals support, opposition, or a procedural request without answering the questions.
proposals.rationale: R02 responds point by point to FDA’s information-collection questions, and R57 evaluates practical utility and data gaps, unlike the extension-only requests in R08 and R40.

proposals.name: Document volume
