proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much extended text, page-level elaboration, or multi-section material is present? Score only extent from the item text; do not judge whether the amount is good, persuasive, accurate, or relevant.
proposals.rationale: Submission capacity and staff time can produce longer documents, independently of substantive merit. Extended multi-page material appears in R06 and R43, while much shorter comments appear in R12 and R44.

proposals.name: Institutional status display
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the text display organizational affiliation, membership scale, office locations, leadership titles, or institutional credentials? Score only extent; do not judge whether the displayed status is good or substantively relevant.
proposals.rationale: Institutional reputation and network may affect reception while leaving recognizable affiliation and scale markers in the text. Such markers appear in R07 and R50, as well as R56.

proposals.name: Professional production markers
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much formal letterhead, legal correspondence structure, contact information, document conventions, or polished signatory presentation is present? Score only extent; do not judge whether the production quality is good or whether the arguments are sound.
proposals.rationale: Access to lawyers, regulatory staff, or professional editors can leave formal production traces that are not themselves substantive quality. These traces are prominent in R04 and R30, and also visible in R16.

proposals.name: Submission packaging complexity
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the item refer to attachments, indexes, batches, joint files, replacement submissions, or multiple supporting documents? Score only extent; do not judge whether the packaging is good or whether the materials are substantively useful.
proposals.rationale: Organizational filing systems and staff capacity can create elaborate submission packaging that affects visibility independently of comment quality. Packaging cues occur in R32 and R46, while replacement or attached-file procedures appear in R25 and R42.

proposals.name: Technical citation density
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much specialized regulatory vocabulary, statutory or regulatory citation, docket cross-reference, technical standard, or numbered provision appears? Score only extent; do not judge whether the terminology is correct, good, or substantively valuable.
proposals.rationale: Professional expertise may leave dense technical fingerprints that can predict reception without being equivalent to substantive quality. Dense citations and standards appear in R04 and R33, and technical cross-references appear in R45.

proposals.name: Personal identity claims
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the text identify the writer’s personal experience, occupation, credentials, residence, affected status, or first-hand relationship to the issue? Score only extent; do not judge whether the experience or identity is good, credible, or relevant.
proposals.rationale: Personal proximity may influence how a comment is received and may also supply genuine information, so the channel is a sensitivity factor rather than a quality criterion. Such claims appear in R20 and R39, and first-hand identity is central in R23.

proposals.name: Coalition mobilization cues
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the text show coordinated participation through joint authorship, named partner organizations, membership appeals, campaign language, or collective representation? Score only extent; do not judge whether the coordination is good or substantively warranted.
proposals.rationale: Campaign networks and organizational coordination can affect visibility while also potentially improving access to information. Joint or coalition markers appear in R21, R43, and R46.

proposals.name: Boilerplate advocacy phrasing
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much repeated formulaic language, stock greetings, standardized requests, generic appreciation, or reusable advocacy wording is present? Score only extent; do not judge whether the wording is good, sincere, persuasive, or relevant.
proposals.rationale: Reusable templates and campaign scripts can predict how a submission is processed without representing substantive merit. Formulaic wording appears in R28 and R36, while standardized extension-request language appears in R31 and R58.

proposals.name: Timing and deadline cues
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much explicit timing information, deadline discussion, extension language, delay explanation, or time-sensitive administrative framing is present? Score only extent; do not judge whether the timing or request is good or justified.
proposals.rationale: Production deadlines, comment-period extensions, and delayed responses can shape both document form and available preparation time, independently of intrinsic quality. These cues appear in R31 and R55, and prominently in R58.

proposals.name: OCR and transcription artifacts
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much scanning, OCR, transcription, encoding, character-substitution, spacing, or visible document-conversion error is present? Score only extent; do not judge whether the artifacts are good, bad, or indicative of substantive quality.
proposals.rationale: Legacy scanning, email extraction, and conversion systems can leave mechanical traces that affect model behavior but have no substantive content value. Such artifacts are visible in R15 and R41, and also in R17 and R57.
